meta.name: pstack map
meta.tagline: if you want to go fast, go deep first. pstack helps you write less, but higher quality code. rigorous agent workflows you can parallelize with confidence.
meta.authors: Lauren Tan (@poteto), Cursor; Claude Code port by Michael Denyer

sources.label: poteto on X: The Complete Guide to pstack Pt. 1

meta.countNote: flavio post says 24 skills/23 principles/22 playbooks (+1 internal); repo README/dir listing show 28 skills, 24 principles, 23 playbook files; marketplace shows 52 skills (=28+24) and 2 subagents.

stages.name: Plan
stages.principle: pstack has **no planning skill, on purpose** ("the best spec is code"). Here, planning means ==understand first==: restate the problem, read how the code works and why, and answer open questions by running something.
when: When a report is vague or noisy → ask /poteto-mode to restate it first, no code yet
When you must change code you do not know → you are in Plan: start with /how
When a job is too big or too risky for one playbook → you are in Plan: /figure-it-out designs the run
When you will walk away and review later → set up the decision log first (/show-me-your-work)
stages.gap: No requirements-gathering, interview or intent-file skill. The closest pieces are the read-only Investigation playbook, the restate-first prompt and the Multi-phase plan playbook (a playbook, not a skill).

sources.label: pstack README (L248: "i don't believe in planning. the best spec is code.")
Guide ch.2 restate a noisy report first (L61-67)
Guide ch.4 plan only after the design settles (L101-117)

stages.name: Design
stages.principle: Settle the **shape of the code** before writing it: sketch how callers use it, let ==several attempts compete==, pick the smaller interface. Answer open questions with a prototype, not a debate. (Code design only. pstack has nothing for UI design.)
when: When new code crosses a function boundary → you are in Design: /architect
When one attempt would lock in the wrong shape → you are in Design: /arena
When an open question can be answered by running something → run the Prototype playbook, not a debate
When a contested design is expensive to reverse → /architect, then /interrogate before shipping

sources.label: Guide ch.4 how much design a task deserves (L119-131)

stages.name: Build
stages.principle: Make the **smallest change the evidence justifies**, test-first when a test is cheap, then ==strip the slop and the comments== before anyone reviews it.
when: When the shape is settled and you start writing → you are in Build
When a bug has a cheap local test path → /tdd, then fix
When you touch .ts or .tsx → /typescript-best-practices
When the diff is ready to commit → /deslop, then /no-comments before review

sources.label: Guide ch.5 /tdd, TypeScript rules and cleanup (L43-81)

stages.name: Test
stages.principle: "It compiles" is not evidence. **Prove it on the real artifact**, ==vet any number== you measured, then have other models attack the diff.
when: When you finished a change → you are in Test: state the finish condition and run the real thing
When nothing can drive the app → /create-verification-skill
When a small diff worries you → /blast-radius
When you measured a speedup → /benchmark-checklist before you report it
When the diff is ready to attack → /interrogate

sources.label: Guide ch.6 numbers and verification skills (L31-94)

stages.name: Deploy
stages.principle: pstack's release step stops at the **merge**: open a ready PR, drive it to merge-ready, then land only the ==contiguous verified run==. It never merges on its own.
when: When the work is verified and you open the PR → you are in Deploy: Opening a PR playbook
When a PR has conflicts, review comments or red CI → /poteto-mode babysit this PR
When you are ready to land a stack → /poteto-mode land the stack (Shipping playbook)
stages.gap: No deploy, rollout, rollback or post-release monitoring skills. Babysit and Shipping end at the merge.

sources.label: Guide ch.6 open the PR, Babysit, Shipping (L96-128)

stages.name: Maintain
stages.principle: Not covered. pstack has **no skills** for watching logs, metrics or errors after release, or for feeding what you learn back into the next plan.
when: When you need to watch production and loop back to Plan → pstack has nothing for this stage
stages.gap: Nothing on monitoring, incident triage, metrics review or the loop back to Plan. The closest pstack ideas are about the agent harness, not the product: see the Anytime band Improve pstack over time (/maintain-verification-skill, /correct, /reflect).

sources.label: Guide ch.9 make it yours (harness upkeep, not product upkeep) (L1-50)

categories.name: Learn the code first
categories.blurb: Read-only: how it works now, why it is shaped that way, and a plain account.
categories.principle: Never edit code you have not traced. ==Mechanics first, history second==, then one plain explanation.
when: When you must change code you do not know → start with how
When a number or choice looks arbitrary → start with why (or do why first, then how)
When you must really understand a PR or subsystem → start with teach, which runs how and why for you
categories.chainWhy: The Investigation playbook runs how first and adds why for motivation questions (investigation.md:7). The guide recipe says mechanics first, history second (guide ch.10 L9-13), and also allows why first when you suspect history explains the mess (guide ch.3 L35). teach sits on top of how and why and weaves them into one account (teach SKILL.md:11).

categories.name: Plan a big or unattended job
categories.blurb: Design a custom playbook and a decision log when no standard playbook fits.
categories.principle: pstack plans with code, not documents. For large or step-away work it ==designs a bespoke, auditable playbook== and logs every decision so a reviewer can follow it later.
when: When no bundled playbook fits → start with figure-it-out
When you will step away and review later → start with figure-it-out; it keeps the show-me-your-work log
When you only need a log for a long run → show-me-your-work alone
categories.chainWhy: poteto-mode routes large, cross-cutting or step-away work to figure-it-out even when a narrower playbook fits (poteto-mode SKILL.md:123), and figure-it-out logs the run via show-me-your-work (figure-it-out SKILL.md:46). Mid-way it calls architect and arena for one-way-door decisions (figure-it-out SKILL.md:30), which belong to Design.

sources.label: Guide ch.7 overnight contract and loop (L18-56)

categories.name: Settle the code shape
categories.blurb: Competing sketches, then adversarial review, before any code locks in.
categories.principle: One attempt locks in the first shape the model thought of. ==Sketch from the caller's side, compete, then attack== the chosen design.
when: When new code crosses a function boundary → start with architect
When one try would lock in the wrong shape (a name, a format, an algorithm) → start with arena
When a contested design is expensive to reverse → architect, then interrogate before shipping
categories.chainWhy: architect grounds with how and why, then runs arena for competing sketches (architect SKILL.md; guide ch.4 L15). The design ladder ends with a contested design getting architect, then interrogate before shipping (guide ch.4 L128). The official mermaid diagram shows the same panel: task -> candidates -> cross-judge -> pick a base -> graft -> verify (guide ch.4 L33-46). interrogate also appears in the Test stage on the finished diff.

sources.label: Guide ch.4 official design-panel mermaid diagram (L33-46)

categories.name: Write it test-first
categories.blurb: Failing test first, then the fix, in typed code that follows the rules.
categories.principle: Say what you observed, let the playbook demand the evidence. Write the ==smallest failing test== when a test is cheap, then the smallest fix.
when: When a bug has a cheap local test path → start with tdd
When the task touches .ts or .tsx → typescript-best-practices
When writing a feature or refactor → the poteto-mode playbook picks the steps; tdd stays optional
categories.chainWhy: The Bug fix playbook stages the failing repro before the fix and points to tdd when a cheap test path exists (bug-fix.md:11). typescript-best-practices is path-scoped and loads when you edit TypeScript (guide ch.5 L53-55). The order of these two is inferred: they do not fire in a fixed sequence in any source.

categories.name: Clean up the diff
categories.blurb: Strip AI leftovers and needless comments before commit and review.
categories.principle: A diff with narrating comments and defensive dead weight reads as unfinished. ==Clean code, then comments, then review.==
when: When you are about to commit AI-written code → start with deslop
When the diff is about to go to review → no-comments (a reviewer who did not write them)
When the diff feels padded → say deslop it before you commit, not after review
categories.chainWhy: poteto-mode: before commit run deslop, before review run no-comments (poteto-mode SKILL.md:28-29). The Opening a PR playbook repeats the order (opening-a-pr.md:9). Prose cleanup (unslop) is in the Anytime Writing band.

sources.label: poteto-mode SKILL.md, before commit / before review (L28-29)
Guide ch.5 clean before you commit (L57-81)

categories.name: Prove it on the real app
categories.blurb: A scripted way to drive the app, then many verifiers at once.
categories.principle: The agent needs a **scripted way to drive your app**. Once it exists, ==fan out one verifier per feature==.
when: When nothing can prove the app works → start with create-verification-skill
When the verify skill works and you want a full pass → swarm, one worker per feature-map entry
categories.chainWhy: create-verification-skill writes the verify-<app> skill and feature map (guide ch.6 L51-61). Once it works, a swarm can split a full pass by feature-map entry (guide ch.6 L73). setup-pstack offers the verification skill once (setup-pstack SKILL.md:72-74). Keep it honest later with maintain-verification-skill (Anytime, Improve pstack over time).

sources.label: Guide ch.6 create a verification skill, then swarm (L51-73)

categories.name: Vet the change and the number
categories.blurb: What could this break, and is this speedup real.
categories.principle: Before you trust a small diff or a measured number, ==prove the one fact it is safe because of==.
when: When a small diff worries you → start with blast-radius
When you measured a speedup or regression → benchmark-checklist before you report it
categories.chainWhy: Guide ch.6 introduces blast-radius (L29) and then benchmark-checklist (L31). The two skills are independent, so this order is the guide's reading order. poteto-mode runs benchmark-checklist before reporting any number (poteto-mode SKILL.md:31), and the Perf issue and Hillclimb playbooks run it themselves.

categories.name: Attack the diff
categories.blurb: Several models review the finished diff, then a harsh maintainability pass.
categories.principle: Different models have different blind spots. ==A finding two models raise on their own is worth acting on.==
when: When a diff is ready to attack → start with interrogate
When you want a harsh maintainability audit → thermo-nuclear-code-quality-review
categories.chainWhy: A subagent that opens a PR runs interrogate, deslop and no-comments (opening-a-pr.md:34). poteto-mode runs interrogate on a contested design before shipping (poteto-mode SKILL.md:24). thermo-nuclear-code-quality-review is a Claude-port-only extra with no place in any playbook, so its slot after interrogate is inferred.

categories.name: Get the PR merged
categories.blurb: Make the PR easy to read, then drive it to merge-ready.
categories.principle: An open PR starts collecting blockers at once. ==Conflicts first, then review threads, then CI==, and every fix batched into one push.
when: When you want reviewers to understand the PR fast → start with make-pr-easy-to-review
When a PR is open and needs shepherding → start with babysit
When there are merge conflicts → fix-merge-conflicts
When you need the review state → get-pr-comments
When CI is red → fix-ci
categories.chainWhy: Babysit works blockers in order: conflicts, then review threads, then CI (babysit.md:11). The Claude port babysit skill delegates to fix-merge-conflicts, fix-ci and get-pr-comments (babysit SKILL.md:31-33; it lists CI before comments, the playbook lists threads before CI, so the playbook order is used). Opening a PR never starts a babysit by itself (opening-a-pr.md:32). make-pr-easy-to-review is not referenced by any playbook, so placing it before babysit is inferred.

sources.label: Guide ch.6 open the PR and Babysit (L96-118)

anytime.blurb: The front door. Type it first and it picks the playbook and calls the other skills.

anytime.name: Setup and help
anytime.blurb: Install, pick models per role, and find the right skill.

anytime.name: Catch up and plain talk
anytime.blurb: Rebuild context, summarize a chat or your commits, restate a reply in plain words.

anytime.name: Writing
anytime.blurb: Prose rules for replies, docs, PR text and commit messages.

anytime.name: Improve pstack over time
anytime.blurb: Turn lessons and repeated mistakes into skill edits and enforced checks; keep the verification skill honest.

anytime.name: Extras (Cursor only)
anytime.blurb: A Cursor-only helper outside the main workflow.

anytime.name: Principles: Keep it small
anytime.blurb: Do less, delete more, make it easy to read.

anytime.name: Principles: Design the shape
anytime.blurb: Think about structure and the user before logic.

anytime.name: Principles: Code structure & safety
anytime.blurb: Where state, validation and types live; safe under retries and concurrency.

anytime.name: Principles: Prove it
anytime.blurb: Check the real thing, test behavior, trace root causes, vet numbers.

anytime.name: Principles: Work well with agents
anytime.blurb: Protect context, keep moving, build tools, encode lessons.

poteto-mode.name: poteto-mode
when: When you have a **real task** and are not sure how to start ==type it first== → [[poteto-mode]]
When a bug, feature, refactor or slow path needs **proof, not guesses** → [[poteto-mode]]
When you are about to **step away** and want the work verified and logged → [[poteto-mode]]
poteto-mode.whatItIs: The **front door** of pstack. It picks the ==right playbook== for your task and runs it for you.
howItWorks: It reads the **list of rules** and finds the playbook that fits your task (1 of 23)
It copies that playbook's steps into a **to-do list**, word for word
It calls ==helper skills== when the playbook says so
It hands code work to **sub-agents**, then reviews every change itself
It writes the final answer in **short, plain** sentences

example.situation: users report duplicate records after a retry.
example.youType: /poteto-mode this command emits two records after a retry. repro first, then fix and verify.
whatHappens: It picks the **Bug fix** playbook and reproduces the bug.
It finds the root cause and fixes it.
example.youGet: A fix plus a short reply: **what broke, why, and the proof**.

behindTheScenes: steps copied into a to-do list
hook sees many files, a design choice or an unknown bug

setup-pstack.name: setup-pstack
when: When you ==just installed pstack== and nothing is configured yet → [[setup-pstack]]
When you want a **cheaper or stronger model** for one job like code or review → [[setup-pstack]]
When the **routing hook** reminds you too often (or not enough) in Claude Code → [[setup-pstack]]
setup-pstack.whatItIs: A setup helper. It chooses **which AI model** does each job, and ==how hard it thinks==.
howItWorks: It lists the **models** you can use
It loads your old choices, or the **defaults**
It asks for a ==budget== (small, medium, large, unlimited) and fills in a model per job
It shows every job so you can **change** any of them
It checks each model name is real, then **saves** the settings

example.situation: you just installed pstack.
whatHappens: It lists the models you can use.
It asks for a budget and fills one model per job.
example.youGet: A **settings file**. Start a new chat to use it.

behindTheScenes: read by every other pstack skill
you add it to `CLAUDE.md` with an @ line
it offers to build a verify skill

poteto-help.name: poteto-help
when: When you are **new** and ==do not know which skill== fits → [[poteto-help]]
When poteto-mode **keeps switching off** between turns → `/poteto-help how do i keep it on?`
When you want a **ready-to-send prompt** for a task → [[poteto-help]]
poteto-help.whatItIs: A **guide** that answers your pstack questions and ==hands you a prompt== to send.
howItWorks: It works out what you need: **set up, start a task, pick a skill, fix a bad run, or customize**
It checks if your **model settings file** exists
It reads the **right guide page** before it quotes it
It replies with an ==answer, a copy-ready prompt, and a link==

example.situation: poteto-mode works once, then you lose it.
example.youType: /poteto-help how do i get poteto-mode to stay on every turn?
whatHappens: It works out what you want.
It reads the right guide page.
example.youGet: An **answer**, a prompt you can send, and a link.

behindTheScenes: it does not start the work

figure-it-out.name: figure-it-out
when: When the job is a **big migration** that no standard playbook covers → [[figure-it-out]]
When you want to ==step away== and trust the result later → [[figure-it-out]]
When a change touches **many places** and you need an audit trail → [[figure-it-out]]
figure-it-out.whatItIs: It **designs a custom playbook** for a job that is too big or odd for the standard ones.
howItWorks: **Frame:** it writes ==what "done" means== as something you can check
**Design:** it splits the work into small units, riskiest first, and builds the check first
For each unit it loops: **guess, smallest change, measure on the real thing, keep or undo**
It **logs every decision** as it goes
At the end it checks the whole result against "done"

example.situation: 40 call sites, no playbook fits.
example.youType: /figure-it-out migrate every caller to the new parser, then delete the old API
whatHappens: It splits the work into small units, riskiest first.
example.youGet: A **custom playbook**, a decision log, and a verified result.

behindTheScenes: final check on the real product

how.name: how
when: When you are about to **change code you do not know** → [[how]]
When you ask **"where should this live?"** or "which package owns this?" → [[how]]
When a bug fix needs you to ==understand the area first== → [[how]]
how.whatItIs: It **explains how part of the code works**, like onboarding a new senior engineer.
howItWorks: It decides: is the question **simple** (one file) or **big** (a whole subsystem)?
Simple: **one explainer** sub-agent reads the code and answers
Big: it splits the question into **2-4 angles** and runs one ==read-only explorer== for each, all at once
Then **one explainer** turns the findings into a write-up

example.situation: you must change notification code you have never read.
example.youType: /how do we dedupe notifications? is there an n+1 when we look up subscribers?
whatHappens: Explorers read the code in parallel.
example.youGet: **Overview, key concepts, how it works, where things live, gotchas**.

why.name: why
when: When a number or limit looks ==arbitrary== ("why is the retry limit five?") → [[why]]
When a change **broke something** and you need the history behind it → [[why]]
When you are about to **delete code** and want to know why it exists → [[why]]
why.whatItIs: It **finds the reasons behind code**: who chose it, what forced it, and ==what we only guess==.
howItWorks: It pins down the **code** you mean and your question
It builds an **anchor**: git blame, git log, PR numbers and PR text
It finds which **tools are connected** (git, tickets, docs, chat, monitoring, errors, analytics)
It runs **one investigator per source**, all at once
One writer merges them and keeps ==facts apart from guesses==
If you plan a change, you also get a **Preserve / Change / Avoid / Risk** list

example.situation: a magic number blocks your change.
example.youType: /why was the retry limit set to five? does the reason still hold?
whatHappens: It blames the line and pulls PRs.
Investigators check tickets, docs and chat.
example.youGet: A **cited report** that keeps facts apart from guesses.

teach.name: teach
when: When a PR or subsystem is **confusing** and you want to ==really get it== → [[teach]]
When the agent picked a design and you ask **"why not a queue?"** → [[teach]]
When you must **explain a change** to someone else → [[teach]]
teach.whatItIs: It **explains work in plain words** so you actually get it.
howItWorks: It picks the **few things** you should walk away knowing
It runs ==how and why together== and blends the results
It starts with a **plain definition**, then ties it to your code
It draws **diagrams one part at a time**, not one giant picture
It stays a **conversation**: short answer first, deeper when you ask

example.situation: you must approve a PR you only half understand.
example.youType: /teach me how this PR changes retries. convince me it fixes the cause and not the symptom.
whatHappens: It draws diagrams one part at a time.
example.youGet: A **plain explanation** you can repeat.

recall.name: recall
when: When you **come back after a few days** and forgot where you stopped → [[recall]]
When you ==start work on a topic== you touched before → [[recall]]
When you need the **latest on a bug** across chats, PRs and tickets → [[recall]]
recall.whatItIs: It **rebuilds what you were doing** from your chats and the team record, then gives a short brief.
howItWorks: It locks the **scope**: time window (default 7 days), topic, this workspace
Cheap sub-agents **search your old chats** for the topic
It uses ==why's investigators== on tickets, chat, docs and errors
It **checks every PR, branch and ticket** with git and gh
It writes a **brief**: summary, tagged threads, problems, one next move

example.situation: you were out for a week.
example.youType: /recall catch me up on the export work from last week
whatHappens: It checks PRs and tickets with git and gh.
example.youGet: A **short brief** with status tags and one next step.

ketchup.name: ketchup
when: When you **return to a long agent chat** and cannot tell what needs you → [[ketchup]]
When several **PRs and agents** ran while you were away → [[ketchup]]
When you ==only need the decisions== that are yours → [[ketchup]]
ketchup.whatItIs: It **catches you up on this chat** since your last message and lists what only you can decide.
howItWorks: It finds your **last real message**
It gathers your work, sub-agent reports and other messages since then
It checks the **live state** of each PR, CI run or agent
It opens with the ==number of action items==, then what happened
Each action item gets: the **decision, options, advice, and what happens if you wait**

example.situation: you left three agents running and went to lunch.
whatHappens: It checks live PR and CI state.
example.youGet: A short catch-up and the **calls only you can make**.

bro.name: bro
when: When the answer is right but ==full of jargon== → [[bro]]
When you must **forward an explanation** to a non-expert → [[bro]]
bro.whatItIs: It **says the last message again** in simple human words.
howItWorks: It takes the agent's **last message**
It **drops the jargon**
It says it again, **shorter and plainer**

example.situation: the agent explained a race condition in dense jargon.
example.youGet: A **short, plain rewrite**.

architect.name: architect
when: When **new code will be used by other code** → [[architect]]
When you are about to ==lock in the shape of your code== (data types, function inputs, files) → [[architect]]
When you care most about **how callers will use it** → [[architect]]
architect.whatItIs: It **sketches the shape first** (data types, function inputs and outputs, files), then fills in the code.
howItWorks: **Ground:** it runs how, and why if ownership changes
**Sketch:** it runs an arena of ==at least two different designs==
It checks each design against a **red-flags list** and prefers the smaller interface
**Agree:** no pause by default; it stops only if you ask for a checkpoint
**Implement:** it replaces the "not implemented" bodies and reports surprises
**Scrap:** if the same workaround keeps coming back, it throws the sketch out

example.situation: a new import pipeline will have many callers.
example.youType: /architect design the import pipeline before writing any code. i care most about how callers use it.
whatHappens: It sketches several shapes from the caller's side.
It picks the smaller one, then fills in code.
example.youGet: A **type and signature sketch** plus the reasons for the choice.

behindTheScenes: rationale file saved next to it

arena.name: arena
when: When **one attempt would lock in the wrong shape** → [[arena]]
When something is ==expensive to change later== (a cache key format, an API) → [[arena]]
When you want **a second opinion** on an approach → [[arena]]
arena.whatItIs: It **runs several agents on the same task**, picks the best, and borrows good parts from the rest.
howItWorks: **Frame:** it writes the artifact, a ==3-6 point rubric==, picks the runners, gives each its own folder
**Fan out:** all candidates start at once, in the background
**Cross-judge:** a read-only judge from a different model family scores them
**Pick:** you read every candidate and choose a base
**Graft:** it ports 1-2 good ideas from each loser, by hand
It **verifies** the final result

example.situation: a cache key format is hard to undo.
example.youType: /arena this, 5 candidates. the cache key format is expensive to change later.
whatHappens: Five agents try it in separate worktrees.
A judge on another model scores them.
You pick a base and graft the best parts.
example.youGet: **One merged result**.

behindTheScenes: the rubric is for the judge

swarm.name: swarm
when: When you must **check many things the same way** (every package, every service) → [[swarm]]
When you want to ==race several approaches== and keep the winner → [[swarm]]
When one agent would take **too long** on independent slices → [[swarm]]
swarm.whatItIs: It **runs many workers at once** and gives you one report.
howItWorks: **Frame:** done-condition, shape (slices or race), count, worker model
**Fan out:** all workers start at once in the cloud, in the background
Each worker reports ==PASS, ISSUES or BLOCKED== with proof
**Aggregate:** it drops results with no proof, retries once, then notes a gap
**Report:** one table, one-line issues, gaps

example.situation: 30 packages need the same check.
example.youType: /swarm check every package under packages/ against its check.sh. one worker per package. one report.
whatHappens: Each reports PASS, ISSUES or BLOCKED.
example.youGet: **One table** of results.

behindTheScenes: get their own folder or worktree

interrogate.name: interrogate
when: When your **change is ready** and you want it attacked before it ships → [[interrogate]]
When people **disagree on a design** and you want outside opinions → [[interrogate]]
When you suspect ==blind spots== in your own review → [[interrogate]]
interrogate.whatItIs: Several **different AI models try to break your change**. You get one judged verdict.
howItWorks: It scopes the **diff or files**
It writes the **intent** in one paragraph
One **read-only reviewer per model** starts at the same time
It merges the findings and notes which models found each
It sorts them: ==Act on, Consider, Noted, Dismissed==, with reasons
It **never applies changes** itself

example.situation: the branch is done and you want it attacked.
example.youType: /interrogate the whole branch, but skeptically. no nitpicks unless it's an actual bug or regression.
whatHappens: Several models review the diff alone.
example.youGet: Findings sorted into **Act on, Consider, Noted, Dismissed**.

tdd.name: tdd
when: When a bug is ==easy to catch with a test== → [[tdd]]
When you want the **failing test first**, then the fix → [[tdd]]
When you want a **test that stops a fixed bug coming back** → [[tdd]]
tdd.whatItIs: It **writes a failing test first**, then fixes the bug. It skips the test if it would be a bad one.
howItWorks: It works out **intended vs current behavior** and the smallest repro
It picks the **narrowest test style** already in the code
It writes the ==smallest failing test==
It runs it and checks it **fails for the right reason**
It makes the smallest fix and **reruns the test**

example.situation: a bug has a cheap local test.
example.youType: /poteto-mode repro the duplicate write first. if there's a cheap test path, /tdd it. then fix and rerun.
whatHappens: It writes the smallest failing test.
example.youGet: A **regression test** and before and after proof.

behindTheScenes: script, browser run or log check instead

typescript-best-practices.name: typescript-best-practices
when: When you **edit a `.ts` or `.tsx` file** → it loads ==on its own==
When the compiler is quiet but you see **casts and loose types** → this skill
typescript-best-practices.whatItIs: A **rule sheet** for typed TypeScript: no casts, no loose types, check data at the edges.
howItWorks: It applies **type-system-discipline** first
It uses **unions, branded types and `unknown`** instead of `any`
It ==parses outside data once==, at the edge
It uses **exhaustive checks** so a new case breaks the build
It prefers **real tests** over mocks

example.situation: you add a handler that reads JSON.
whatHappens: Outside data is parsed once at the edge.
example.youGet: Code with **no casts and checked edges**.

unslop.name: unslop
when: When a **reply, doc or PR text** reads like AI → [[unslop]]
When you see ==em dashes, filler and hedging== → [[unslop]]
When you are about to **publish** a README → [[unslop]]
unslop.whatItIs: It **strips the AI-sounding habits** from any text.
howItWorks: It scans for **numbered patterns**: AI words, em dashes, filler, hedging
It rewrites each hit in **plain words**
It ==keeps the meaning and tone==
It prefers **active voice** and whole sentences

example.situation: your README update sounds like a chatbot.
whatHappens: It rewrites each in plain words.
example.youGet: The **same text** without the AI tells.

behindTheScenes: poteto-mode runs it on every reply
other skills cite its rule numbers

technical-writing.name: technical-writing
when: When you **write or review** a README, RFC or PR description → [[technical-writing]]
When a doc ==mixes a tutorial with reference== → [[technical-writing]]
When a **commit message** needs to be clear → [[technical-writing]]
technical-writing.whatItIs: A **writing standard** that keeps docs clear and one-purpose.
howItWorks: It picks ==one mode== first: tutorial, how-to, reference or explanation
It writes **direct sentences** to the reader, present tense
One **step per sentence** for instructions
It removes anything that can be **read two ways**
It **varies sentence length**

example.situation: a README mixes a tutorial and reference.
example.youGet: A **clearer README**.

sources.label: poteto-mode SKILL.md, docs and PR text (L27)

no-comments.name: no-comments
when: When the diff is full of **noisy comments** and you are about to ask for review → [[no-comments]]
When a comment explains **code that should be fixed instead** → [[no-comments]]
When a "do not remove" comment ==should be a test or lint== → [[no-comments]]
no-comments.whatItIs: It **deletes needless comments** and fixes the code that needed them.
howItWorks: It takes your **files or the diff** against main
It starts the **Comment Sicko** sub-agent to flag and delete comments
It ==checks the work== and puts back any wrong deletion
It fixes flagged code, or runs architect if a new shape is needed
It offers a **lint, type or test** to replace "do not remove" comments

example.situation: the diff has 40 new comments.
whatHappens: The lead restores any wrong deletion.
example.youGet: A **cleaner diff** and a short report.

behindTheScenes: fix the code or offer a lint/test
edits comments only, never app code

deslop.name: deslop
when: When you are **about to commit** AI-written code → [[deslop]]
When you see **odd try/catch, [[any]] casts or deep nesting** → [[deslop]]
When you want a ==leaner diff== with no behavior change → [[deslop]]
deslop.whatItIs: It **removes the leftovers** AI code tends to add.
howItWorks: It checks the **diff against main**
It removes **extra comments, odd try/catch, `any` casts and deep nesting**
It ==keeps behavior the same==
It gives a **1-3 sentence** summary

example.situation: you are about to commit AI-written code.
whatHappens: It checks the diff against main.
It removes extra comments and odd casts.
example.youGet: A **leaner diff** and a 1-3 sentence summary.

create-verification-skill.name: create-verification-skill
when: When your project has **no scripted way** to prove the app works → [[create-verification-skill]]
When agents ==keep claiming it works== without running it → [[create-verification-skill]]
When you want **video and screenshot proof** of a change → [[create-verification-skill]]
create-verification-skill.whatItIs: It **builds a skill** that lets future agents run your app like a user and capture proof.
howItWorks: It **reads the repo** (not you) for how to launch, drive and capture proof
It writes `verify-<app>/SKILL.md`: ==Launch, Doctor, Drive, Evidence, Cleanup, Helpers==
It adds a **features/** folder, one file per feature
It **runs its own steps once**, end to end
It points you to the maintain skill

example.situation: nobody can prove the app works.
example.youGet: A **tested verify skill** with a feature map.

maintain-verification-skill.name: maintain-verification-skill
when: When the **verify skill no longer matches** the app → [[maintain-verification-skill]]
When you ==shipped new features== since it was written → [[maintain-verification-skill]]
When you want a **daily upkeep** routine for it → [[maintain-verification-skill]]
maintain-verification-skill.whatItIs: It **checks the verify skill against the real app** and fixes drift in one PR.
howItWorks: It finds the verify skill and **tidies its index**
**Source wave:** one read-only sub-agent per feature
It reconciles results and ==sweeps recent changes== for missing features
**Live pass:** it drives every feature in the real app
**Triage:** doc drift, harness gap, or product bug
It ships **one PR**, or reports clean or blocked

example.situation: three new features shipped since the verify skill was written.
whatHappens: Readers check each feature in code.
example.youGet: **One PR** of proven fixes, or clean.

behindTheScenes: live pass in the real app
edits only the verify skill folder

benchmark-checklist.name: benchmark-checklist
when: When a **speedup looks too good** to be true → [[benchmark-checklist]]
When you are about to ==put a number in a PR== → [[benchmark-checklist]]
When two runs **disagree** and you do not know why → [[benchmark-checklist]]
benchmark-checklist.whatItIs: It **checks a speed measurement** before you trust or report it.
howItWorks: It writes the **claim** you expect to make
It reads the script and checks the **machine load**
It asks **7 questions**: why not double, tuned, limits, errors, repeatable, real-world, did the work run
It runs each side **5+ times**, alternating
It gives a ==verdict== with the number, run count, range and limiter

example.situation: a 40% speedup looks too good.
example.youType: /benchmark-checklist vet the export speedup before it goes in the pr
example.youGet: A **verdict** with the number, run count and limiter.

behindTheScenes: used by the Perf and Hillclimb playbooks

blast-radius.name: blast-radius
when: When a **tiny diff** worries you → [[blast-radius]]
When a brief says =="X already handles Y"== and you must trust it → [[blast-radius]]
When you ask **"what could this break?"** → [[blast-radius]]
blast-radius.whatItIs: It **finds what a change could break elsewhere**, then proves why it is safe by running code.
howItWorks: It reads the diff, **including what it does not say**
It finds the ==one fact== the change is safe because of
It looks where grep stops: library code, timing, file formats, flags, other languages
It rates each risk: **chance, cost, file:line**
It writes and **runs a small script** that proves the key fact
On a big change it runs an arena

example.situation: a tiny diff touches shared code.
example.youType: /blast-radius this one-line change to the retry timeout
whatHappens: It finds the one fact the change is safe because of.
It runs a script to prove it.
example.youGet: A **write-up** of risks and a pre-merge test.

behindTheScenes: "you said so" to "reproduced in the app"

thermo-nuclear-code-quality-review.name: thermo-nuclear-code-quality-review
when: When you want a ==harsh maintainability audit== of a branch → [[thermo-nuclear-code-quality-review]]
When a file keeps **growing past 1000 lines** → [[thermo-nuclear-code-quality-review]]
When conditionals **pile up** like spaghetti → [[thermo-nuclear-code-quality-review]]
thermo-nuclear-code-quality-review.whatItIs: An **extra-harsh review** of structure that pushes for big simplifications.
howItWorks: It runs the **baseline review** on the branch's changes
It hunts for =="code judo"==: one restructure that deletes whole branches or layers
It flags **files over 1000 lines**, bolted-on conditionals, thin wrappers, casts
It suggests fixes like **deleting a layer** or using a typed model
It replies direct and demanding

example.situation: one file passed 1000 lines.
whatHappens: It hunts for a restructure that deletes layers.
example.youGet: A **strict review** with structural fixes.

babysit.name: babysit
when: When you **open a PR** and want it looked after until every check passes → [[babysit]]
When failing checks, clashing edits and ==review comments pile up== → [[babysit]]
When you do not want to **re-prompt** every hour → [[babysit]]
babysit.whatItIs: It **watches an open PR** and fixes clashing edits, failing checks and easy comments until it can merge.
howItWorks: It reads the PR with **gh pr view**
It handles ==conflicts, then CI, then review comments, then bot comments==
It re-checks on a **timer** until green and clean
After **three failed rounds** it stops and hands back
It reports fixes, deferred comments and status

example.situation: you just opened a PR.
whatHappens: It fixes conflicts, then CI, then comments.
example.youGet: A **merge-ready PR**, or a note on what blocks it.

behindTheScenes: never edits tests just to pass

fix-ci.name: fix-ci
when: When a test ==passes on your machine but fails in CI== → [[fix-ci]]
When a PR check turns **red** after a push → [[fix-ci]]
When you do not want to **dig through logs** yourself → [[fix-ci]]
fix-ci.whatItIs: It **finds failing checks** and fixes them one at a time.
howItWorks: It finds the PR and runs **gh pr checks**
It pulls the ==first real error== from the failed logs
It makes the **smallest safe fix**
It pushes, rechecks, and **repeats until green**

example.situation: the test passes locally but CI is red.
whatHappens: It fixes the first real error and pushes.
example.youGet: **Green CI**, or the next failing job.

fix-merge-conflicts.name: fix-merge-conflicts
when: When your branch ==conflicts with main== → [[fix-merge-conflicts]]
When a **lockfile conflict** blocks the merge → [[fix-merge-conflicts]]
When you want the **build and tests rerun** after resolving → [[fix-merge-conflicts]]
fix-merge-conflicts.whatItIs: It **resolves conflicts** without asking, then checks the build still works.
howItWorks: It lists the **conflicted files**
It fixes each with the **smallest correct edit**
It rebuilds **lockfiles** with the package manager
It runs **compile, lint and tests**
It stages the files and ==does not push==

example.situation: main moved and your branch conflicts.
example.youGet: **Resolved files**, staged but not pushed.

get-pr-comments.name: get-pr-comments
when: When reviewers left **a pile of comments** → [[get-pr-comments]]
When you want ==what to fix first== sorted by severity → [[get-pr-comments]]
When you need the **review state** at a glance → [[get-pr-comments]]
get-pr-comments.whatItIs: It **pulls the review comments** and sorts them into an action list.
howItWorks: It finds the **PR for your branch**
It fetches review and discussion comments
It ==groups them by severity==
It returns an **action list**

example.situation: four reviewers commented.
example.youGet: An **action list**.

make-pr-easy-to-review.name: make-pr-easy-to-review
when: When you open a PR and ==nobody reviews it because it is huge== → [[make-pr-easy-to-review]]
When the history is **noisy** (fix typo, fix typo again) → [[make-pr-easy-to-review]]
When reviewers need a **TL;DR** and a reading order → [[make-pr-easy-to-review]]
make-pr-easy-to-review.whatItIs: It **tidies a PR** so reviewers get the point fast. The code behaves the same.
howItWorks: It reads commits, diff size, generated files and the description
It spots **noisy or mixed commits**
It **proposes a plan** before it rewrites history
It applies it and checks the ==final code tree is identical==
It adds a **TL;DR** and reviewer notes

example.situation: a 2,000-line PR sits unreviewed.
whatHappens: It checks the code tree is identical.
example.youGet: A **tidier PR** with a TL;DR.

what-did-i-get-done.name: what-did-i-get-done
when: When **standup** is in five minutes → `/what-did-i-get-done yesterday`
When you owe a ==weekly status update== → `/what-did-i-get-done last week`
what-did-i-get-done.whatItIs: It **turns your recent commits** into a short update.
howItWorks: It turns "yesterday" or "last week" into **real dates**
It reads **your commits** in that range
It skips merge commits and ==uncommitted work==
It writes a tight summary with the real date range

example.situation: weekly update is due.
whatHappens: It turns the dates into a range.
example.youGet: A **short status update** with 2-5 bullets.

show-me-your-work.name: show-me-your-work
when: When you **go to bed** and want agents to keep working → [[show-me-your-work]]
When you must ==trust work you did not watch== → [[show-me-your-work]]
When you return and ask **"what did it do last night?"** → [[show-me-your-work]]
show-me-your-work.whatItIs: It **keeps a log of every decision** so you can trust work you did not watch.
howItWorks: It starts a **TSV log**: time, phase, decision, why, evidence, result
It adds a row at each ==decision, finished unit, pivot or blocker==
It **never edits old rows**; a wrong call gets a new row
At the end it checks the log against the transcript
A different-model reviewer **flags weak evidence**

example.situation: an agent worked overnight.
example.youType: /show-me-your-work catch me up on what you did last night
whatHappens: It checks it against the transcript.
example.youGet: A **decision table** you can audit.

behindTheScenes: kept out of git unless a reviewer needs it

reflect.name: reflect
when: When a **long task finally landed** and you want the lessons kept → [[reflect]]
When a run ==took far too long== and you want it faster next time → [[reflect]]
When you want **skill edits** proposed from a chat → [[reflect]]
reflect.whatItIs: It **turns what went right or wrong** in a chat into real edits to your skills.
howItWorks: It finds this chat's **transcript**
It starts **three reviewers** at once: judgment, tooling, divergent
One writer sorts findings: ==Accepted, Rejected, Backlog==
Anything a lint or script could enforce goes to **Backlog**
It **waits for your OK** before editing

example.situation: a task finished after hours of wrong turns.
example.youType: /reflect that took way too long. capture what we learned so the next run doesn't repeat it.
example.youGet: **Skill edits** you approved.

correct.name: correct
when: When you **keep fixing the same agent mistake** → [[correct]]
When agents ==bypass your repository layer== or skip the schema → [[correct]]
When a rule written in docs gets **ignored** → [[correct]]
correct.whatItIs: It **finds repeated mistakes** and makes each one impossible.
howItWorks: It reads commits, reverts, comments and agent rules for **repeats**
It groups them (a class counts after ==two repeats==)
For each it tries **architecture, types, lint, tests, docs last**
It proves each new check **fails on a real past mistake**
It keeps a **rule-to-enforcer table**

example.situation: the same mistake in every PR.
example.youType: /correct agents keep calling the database client directly instead of going through the repository layer
whatHappens: It proves it fails on a real past mistake.
example.youGet: A **check that fails** on the mistake.

behindTheScenes: strongest fix: architecture > types > lint > test > docs
prove it catches a real mistake
same command runs locally and in CI

automate-me.name: automate-me
when: When you want ==pstack in your own style== → [[automate-me]]
When your **own mode skill is out of date** → `/automate-me update my mode skill`
When you repeat the **same preferences** every session → [[automate-me]]
automate-me.whatItIs: It **builds your own "name-mode" skill** from how you work.
howItWorks: It looks for an existing **-mode skill**
It mines your recent chats in **parallel slices**
It asks a few **multiple-choice questions**
It groups what it found into sections
It drafts the skill, **tightens the prose**, and lands it in a PR

example.situation: you repeat the same preferences each session.
example.youGet: A **personal mode skill** in a PR.

make-bot-ui.name: make-bot-ui
when: When you want a **button page** that wakes a Cursor bot → [[make-bot-ui]]
When a webhook should ==trigger the bot from a dashboard== → [[make-bot-ui]]
make-bot-ui.whatItIs: It **builds a small web page** whose buttons wake a Cursor bot through a webhook.
howItWorks: It creates a **webhook routine**
You copy the **URL and sender key** from the routine panel
It asks for the key with a **secret card**
It hosts the page **on your computer**
It sends a ==test POST== before it says the page is live

example.situation: you want a dashboard button to wake a bot.
example.youGet: A **button page** that wakes your bot.

principle-laziness-protocol.name: laziness-protocol
when: You are **refactoring**, sizing a diff, or ==tempted to add layers==. → apply [[principle-laziness-protocol]]
principle-laziness-protocol.whatItIs: **Delete first.** Make the ==smallest change== that solves it.
howItWorks: Look for deletions before additions
Make the smallest diff that solves it
Question any plan to thread a new flag through many layers

when: Before you **write logic**: choosing types, setting up, or sharing state between actors. → apply [[principle-foundational-thinking]]
principle-foundational-thinking.whatItIs: Get the **data shapes** and the base setup right ==before the logic==.
howItWorks: Define core types first
Do shared setup (CI, test infra, types) before features
Before sharing state between actors, ask what happens if another changes it

sources.label: Guide ch.8 steer with principle names (L1-27)

principle-redesign-from-first-principles.name: redesign-from-first-principles
when: You add a **new requirement** to an existing design. → apply [[principle-redesign-from-first-principles]]
principle-redesign-from-first-principles.whatItIs: Redesign as if the new need had been there ==from day one==.
howItWorks: Read all affected files
Ask what you would build from scratch
Update every reference: types, docs, examples

sources.label: Guide ch.8 steer with principle names (L1-27)

principle-attack-the-premise.name: attack-the-premise
when: **Two fixes** that share one assumption have both failed. → apply [[principle-attack-the-premise]]
howItWorks: Write the shared premise in one sentence
Count which actors hold the imbalance with a rerunnable script
Remove the asymmetry instead of compensating for it

sources.label: Guide ch.8 steer with principle names (L1-27)

principle-subtract-before-you-add.name: subtract-before-you-add
when: You plan an **addition, refactor or rewrite**. → apply [[principle-subtract-before-you-add]]
principle-subtract-before-you-add.whatItIs: **Remove dead weight first**, then build on the ==simpler base==.
howItWorks: Delete dead code before adding
Design for what is used, not edge cases nobody hit
Drop references with no new content

sources.label: Guide ch.8 steer with principle names (L1-27)

principle-minimize-reader-load.name: minimize-reader-load
when: Code is **hard to trace** while you review or shape it. → apply [[principle-minimize-reader-load]]
principle-minimize-reader-load.whatItIs: Judge code by ==how much a reader must trace and remember==.
howItWorks: Inline one-caller wrappers
Shrink state scope (locals over fields over globals)
Test: can a newcomer answer 'where does X come from' in 30 seconds

sources.label: Guide ch.8 steer with principle names (L1-27)

principle-outcome-oriented-execution.name: outcome-oriented-execution
when: A **planned rewrite or migration** with clear phases. → apply [[principle-outcome-oriented-execution]]
principle-outcome-oriented-execution.whatItIs: Aim at the ==final design==, not smooth in-between states.
howItWorks: Break things on purpose only when planned, scoped and reversible
Skip throwaway compatibility code
Run full checks at the end of the plan

sources.label: Guide ch.8 steer with principle names (L1-27)

principle-experience-first.name: experience-first
when: You weigh **product, UX or scope** tradeoffs. → apply [[principle-experience-first]]
howItWorks: Justify every feature and option
Ship fewer things, polished

sources.label: Guide ch.8 steer with principle names (L1-27)

principle-exhaust-the-design-space.name: exhaust-the-design-space
when: A **new idea or design** with no precedent. → apply [[principle-exhaust-the-design-space]]
principle-exhaust-the-design-space.whatItIs: Build **2-3 real alternatives** and ==compare them side by side==.
howItWorks: Make competing prototypes or sketches
Compare them side by side
Skip for mechanical work with one viable way

sources.label: Guide ch.8 steer with principle names (L1-27)

principle-build-the-lever.name: build-the-lever
when: Any **non-trivial work**, not only bulk jobs. → apply [[principle-build-the-lever]]
principle-build-the-lever.whatItIs: Build the ==tool or script== that does the job or proves it.
howItWorks: Do one unit by hand, then write the tool and diff it against the hand version

If you cite this principle, the diff must contain the tool

principle-model-the-domain.name: model-the-domain
when: You write **stateful code**, or code full of if-statements and repeated assumptions. → apply [[principle-model-the-domain]]
principle-model-the-domain.whatItIs: Put the real rules in a ==data structure==, not scattered ifs.
howItWorks: Use a state machine, typed model, registry or reducer
Pick the structure when you write it, not in a later refactor
Organize modules by knowledge, not by execution order

principle-boundary-discipline.name: boundary-discipline
when: You wire up **validation, errors or framework adapters**. → apply [[principle-boundary-discipline]]

Keep business logic in pure functions, framework wiring thin

sources.label: Guide ch.8 steer with principle names (L1-27)

principle-type-system-discipline.name: type-system-discipline
when: You design **types or a signature** in a typed language. → apply [[principle-type-system-discipline]]
howItWorks: Use sum types, not bags of optional fields
Brand IDs and other semantic primitives
Parse outside data once; avoid casts

sources.label: Guide ch.8 steer with principle names (L1-27)

principle-make-operations-idempotent.name: make-operations-idempotent
when: Commands or loops that may hit **crashes and retries**. → apply [[principle-make-operations-idempotent]]
principle-make-operations-idempotent.whatItIs: Running it **again or after a crash** must reach the ==same end state==.
howItWorks: Ask: what if this runs twice, or crashed halfway
Scan and clean stale state on startup
Use self-healing locks

principle-migrate-callers-then-delete-le.name: migrate-callers-then-delete-legacy-apis
when: You add a **new internal API** while old callers still exist. → apply [[principle-migrate-callers-then-delete-legacy-apis]]

Keep adapters only if time-boxed
Update tests to the new contract

when: **Several actors** might write the same file, branch or key. → apply [[principle-separate-before-serializing-shared-state]]

Lock only when one shared target is a real rule

principle-prove-it-works.whatItIs: Check the ==real thing==, not a stand-in like "it compiles".

principle-never-block-on-the-human.name: never-block-on-the-human
when: You want to ask "**should I do X?**" on work you can undo. → apply [[principle-never-block-on-the-human]]
principle-never-block-on-the-human.whatItIs: On undoable work, ==act first==. Let the human correct later.
howItWorks: Proceed, then present
Ask only before irreversible actions
Product direction still comes from the human

playbooks.name: investigation
playbooks.summary: a read-only question. how does x work, why was y built this way, are we sure.
playbooks.whatItIs: Answer a read-only question with sources.
steps: Write the how-shaped answer or a tradeoffs table

playbooks.name: bug fix
playbooks.summary: reproduce a defect, root-cause it, and fix with runtime evidence.
playbooks.whatItIs: Reproduce, find the root cause, and fix it with runtime evidence.
steps: Reproduce yourself on the real surface
Binary-search the cause using how and why
Plan the fix (architect if it crosses a function); delegate to a sub-agent
Commit failing repro before the fix

playbooks.name: perf
playbooks.summary: trace a measured slowness and improve it against a baseline.
playbooks.whatItIs: Trace a measured slowness and improve it against a baseline.
steps: Capture and vet a baseline with benchmark-checklist
Ground with how; try the 'do less/later/cheaper' mantras in order
Cite the number in the PR

playbooks.name: hillclimb
playbooks.summary: sustained, scientific improvement of one metric against a target, looping hypotheses with before/after measurement and one commit per accepted win.
playbooks.whatItIs: Improve one metric step by step with a frozen harness and a decision log.
steps: Build and freeze the measurement harness
Loop one hypothesis at a time; keep or revert
Push past plateaus; stop at target
Open a PR with the kept commits stacked

playbooks.name: runtime forensics
playbooks.summary: diagnose a live symptom (leak, idle-cpu spin, glitch) from instrumentation.
playbooks.whatItIs: Diagnose a live runtime symptom (leak, idle CPU) from instrumentation.
steps: Capture the live signal (profile, heap snapshot, trace)
Hand back a diagnosis, not a fix

playbooks.name: trace forensics
playbooks.summary: diagnose a captured profiling artifact (cpuprofile, trace, spindump, heap snapshot).
playbooks.whatItIs: Diagnose a captured profile or trace after the fact.
steps: Identify the format and load it with the right tool
Narrow to the hot path or retainer chain
Diff before/after if you have both

playbooks.name: feature
playbooks.summary: new or changed behavior, built from a named data shape.
playbooks.whatItIs: Build new behavior from a named data shape.
steps: interrogate if contested; open a PR

playbooks.name: refactoring
playbooks.summary: a behavior-preserving change to structure or shape.
playbooks.whatItIs: Change structure without changing behavior.
steps: Pin behavior with a characterization test
Name the missing structure and target shape
Move in small steps that keep the pin green
Keep it only if reader load dropped

playbooks.name: prototype
playbooks.summary: a throwaway sketch to make a design or behavioral decision cheaply, or to settle an empirical fork by observing it.
playbooks.whatItIs: Build a throwaway sketch to decide something cheaply.
steps: Gather references if the space is open
Build in a scratch dir behind a variant switcher
Verify each variant on the real surface

playbooks.name: visual parity
playbooks.summary: pixel-exact ui equivalence between two implementations.
playbooks.whatItIs: Match two UIs pixel for pixel.
steps: Migrate one component at a time, one owner each

playbooks.name: authoring a skill
playbooks.summary: writing or editing a SKILL.md.
playbooks.whatItIs: Write or edit a SKILL.md.

playbooks.name: eval
playbooks.summary: test how a skill or prompt change affects agent behavior, blinded.

steps: Run N candidates on different models

playbooks.name: babysit
playbooks.summary: drive a pr or a stack to merge-ready: conflicts, review threads, ci.
playbooks.whatItIs: Drive a PR or stack to merge-ready.
steps: Work the lowest unmerged PR first
One babysitter per stack; never change stack topology
Triage Bugbot skeptically; stop at the human's line

playbooks.name: shipping
playbooks.summary: independently verify a green stack, then land the contiguous verified run bottom-up through github by default or origin when available.
playbooks.whatItIs: Land a green stack safely.
steps: Land only the contiguous verified run from the bottom
Check each verdict still matches the patch
Land one PR at a time

playbooks.name: autonomous run
playbooks.summary: drive a long task to completion without stopping.
playbooks.whatItIs: Drive a long task to a checkable finish.
steps: Pick a wake mechanism (watcher or heartbeat)
Make one small change per iteration and verify
Stop only when the predicate is met

Install the runtime (orch init) and open the trail
Pilot one unit end to end
Scale with a rolling window of workers

steps: One owner per PR, in parallel
Owner merges on a clean verdict
